lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What's this, Alexander? Died too, have you, like the rest of us?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: You see, Diogenes. No surprise if a man dies.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So Ammon was lying when he claimed you as his son? You were Philip's all along?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Philip's, of course. I wouldn't have died if I were Ammon's.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And the same stories about Olympias — a dragon consorting with her, seen in her bed, and that's how you were born, with Philip fooled into thinking you were his.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I heard those stories the same as you. Now I see neither my mother nor the Ammon prophets were telling the truth.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Still, their lie served you well enough. Plenty bowed, thinking you a god.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But tell me — who did you leave that vast empire to?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I don't know, Diogenes. I didn't have time to make any arrangements, except handing the ring to Perdiccas as I died. Why are you laughing?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What else? It reminded me how Greece carried on — flattering you the moment you took power, voting you protector and general against the barbarians, some even adding you to the twelve gods, building temples and sacrificing to the dragon's son.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell me, where did the Macedonians bury you?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Still lying in Babylon — thirtieth day now. Ptolemy the bodyguard says when he gets a break from the troubles on the ground, he'll ship me to Egypt and bury me there so I can join the Egyptian gods.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I shouldn't laugh then, Alexander, watching you still playing the fool in Hades, hoping to become Anubis or Osiris? Don't count on it, most divine. No one who's once crossed the lake and passed the mouth is allowed back up. Aeacus isn't careless, and Cerberus isn't to be despised.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But I'd like to know from you — how do you take it when you remember all the happiness you left behind? Bodyguards and hypaspists and satraps, all that gold, nations bowing down, Babylon and Bactra, the great beasts, the honor, the glory, riding out with the white ribbon in your hair and the purple cloak pinned at the shoulder? Doesn't it pain you when it comes back to you? Why the tears, you fool? Didn't even the wise Aristotle teach you not to think fortune's gifts are secure?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: The wise one? The most shameless flatterer of them all. Let me alone know Aristotle's ways — what he begged from me, what letters he wrote, how he played my love of learning to flatter and praise me, now for my looks (as if that counted as virtue), now for my deeds and wealth. And he thought that was a virtue too, so he could take it without shame. A charlatan, Diogenes, and a craftsman at it. But this much I got from his wisdom: to grieve over those greatest goods I just listed.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Well, here's what you'll do. I'll prescribe a cure for your grief. Hellebore doesn't grow here, so drink the water of Lethe — drink deep, drink again, drink often. That'll stop you mourning Aristotle's goods. And look, there's Cleitus and Callisthenes and a crowd of others coming for you, ready to tear you apart and pay you back for what you did to them. So take the other path and drink often, as I said.
